item.aggregated_output:
<<18:42 update 1, part 0 of 0..2>>
## THE CURRENT MAP
18:42/q01 What does وَأُحِيطَ بِثَمَرِهِۦ say happened? [وَأُحِيطَ بِثَمَرِهِۦ · interpretation]
  18:42/q01/p1 The garden's produce or wealth was completely destroyed. — reasons: Ibn Qutayba, al-Kashshaf, Ibn Atiyya, al-Razi, al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi, Abu Hayyan, Bursevi, al-Alusi and Tabataba'i explain the image through an enemy encircling and overpowering someone; al-Wahidi compares 2:81, al-Razi and Abu Hayyan 12:66, and Tabataba'i 10:22. Ibn Qutayba's Mushkil says an encircled town approaches ruin. Al-Tabari recalls the owner's confidence in 18:35; al-Mawardi, Ibn Kathir, Abu Hayyan, Bursevi and Study Quran connect the event with the brother's warning. Al-Biqa'i says the passive makes ruin comprehensive and easy without naming an agent. Al-Dahhak attributes it to God's decree; al-Zajjaj, al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi to God's punishment. Al-Asamm's context in al-Jishumi allows all produce or all wealth. Ibn Atiyya calls it comprehensive punishment; al-Khafaji likens it to a surrounded people annihilated.
18:42/q02 What does ثَمَرِهِۦ encompass? [بِثَمَرِهِۦ · referent] (turns on: Whether the vocalization and the owner's investment point to edible yield, the productive trees, or his entire fortune.)
  18:42/q02/p1 The owner's wealth and all the garden's assets, including produce and property. — reasons: Qatada includes fruit and other property; Mujahid and Ibn Mujahid's father specify gold and silver. Abu Amr includes garden, property, palms and trees under both vocalizations. Al-Wahidi and most exegetes prefer the broad sense because spending went to productive assets; the narrow crop was already established in 18:33–34, whereas the broad term covers fruit and roots. Salam distinguishes one reading for wealth and one for plural fruits; Yunus treats them as equivalent, a conflation al-Wahidi rejects. The Qiraat-ER account calls thumr economic wealth; al-Alusi says the known wealth of both gardens and their contents.
  18:42/q02/p2 The fruit or crop of the gardens, including its several kinds. — reasons: Al-Tha'labi says every kind of fruit; al-Wahidi reports that the common thamar denotes edible fruit and Abu Ishaq prefers it because 18:33 had already mentioned produce. Salam calls the alternative plural fruits, while Yunus equates the forms, against al-Wahidi's distinction. Qiraat-ER calls thamar collective produce and thumur a plural highlighting varieties. Ibn Kathir allows fruits before giving wealth as another interpretation.
  18:42/q02/p3 The fruit-bearing trees and date palms themselves. — reasons: Ibn Zayd in al-Wahidi identifies the trees; Ibn Abbas says the fruit trees and palms, and al-Wahidi argues that investment chiefly goes into the trees and roots. Al-Wahidi's Wajiz says the fruitful trees were destroyed; al-Tabrisi speaks of total ruin of trees and palms.
18:42/q03 How is ثَمَرِهِۦ read, and what do the forms suggest? [بِثَمَرِهِۦ · readings] (turns on: The consonants' vowels and whether the resulting noun is collective fruit, a plural, or wealth; reports differ by reader and occurrence.)
  18:42/q03/p1 Thumur, with ḍamma on both thāʾ and mīm. — reasons: Ibn Mujahid names Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, Hamza and al-Kisa'i; Abu Hayyan adds Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Medinan readers. Al-Nashr assigns it to the remaining readers in both occurrences, and Abu Hayyan records Ruways transmitting this form in the first occurrence but fath in bi-thamarihi. Ibn Khalawayh explains it as a plural of a plural; Abu Hayyan says plural of thimar; Qiraat-ER says plural thamar emphasizing fruit types. Some Abu Amr transmissions agree with Nafi'.
  18:42/q03/p2 Thamar, with fatḥa on both thāʾ and mīm. — reasons: Ibn Mujahid names 'Asim; Abu Hayyan also names Abu Ja'far, al-Hasan, Jabir ibn Zayd, al-Hajjaj, Abu Hatim and Ya'qub through Ruways. Al-Nashr lists Abu Ja'far, 'Asim and Rawh in both occurrences, Ruways in the first only. Ibn Khalawayh describes a collective with singular ending in ta'; Qiraat-ER calls it collective fruit or produce. Abu Ishaq in al-Wahidi favors thamar in view of 18:33.
  18:42/q03/p3 Thumr, with ḍamma on thāʾ and sukūn on mīm. — reasons: Ibn Mujahid and al-Nashr assign it to Abu 'Amr, though Ibn Mujahid notes transmissions matching Nafi'. Abu Hayyan also names al-A'mash and Abu Raja' and explains it as lightened or as a plural of thamarah. Ibn Khalawayh connects it with invested wealth; Qiraat-ER calls it property.
18:42/q04 How is the passive وَأُحِيطَ بِثَمَرِهِۦ parsed? [وَأُحِيطَ بِثَمَرِهِۦ · grammar] (turns on: Whether the understood passive subject is an omitted verbal noun or the bi-phrase in nominative function.)
  18:42/q04/p1 An implicit verbal noun is the passive subject, with the genitive sometimes construed as nominative. — reasons: Al-Nahhas and al-Qurtubi give this analysis; al-Nahhas also calls 'he began turning' a circumstantial accusative. Al-Biqa'i says leaving the agent unnamed conveys the ease and completeness of the destruction.
  18:42/q04/p2 ثَمَرِهِۦ, though introduced by bi-, functions as the nominative passive subject. — reasons: Al-Jishumi expressly gives this parse; al-Nahhas and al-Qurtubi allow the genitive form to have nominative function.
18:42/q05 What rhetorical figure is the encompassing of the fruit? [وَأُحِيطَ بِثَمَرِهِۦ · rhetoric] (turns on: Whether the transfer from encirclement to destruction is classified as metaphor or metonymy.)
  18:42/q05/p1 It is a metaphor of an enemy surrounding and destroying someone. — reasons: Al-Kashshaf, Ibn Atiyya, al-Razi, al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi, Abu Hayyan, Bursevi, al-Alusi and Tabataba'i explain the transfer from military encirclement; al-Khafaji calls it a representative metaphor of a surrounded people annihilated.
  18:42/q05/p2 It is more apparently metonymy for complete destruction. — reasons: Al-Alusi favors this classification over the proposed kinds of metaphor.
18:42/q06 What does the root of أُحِيطَ and the related garden name convey? [وَأُحِيطَ · meaning] (turns on: The literal enclosing sense and its extension to a garden's name or to annihilation.)
  18:42/q06/p1 Iḥāṭa literally surrounds from every side and here extends to destruction. — reasons: Ibn al-Jawzi's Nuzha defines surrounding; Ibn Qutayba's Mushkil likens impending ruin to an encircled enemy or town. Al-Damghani and Ibn al-Jawzi list destruction as a sense, with the overtaking sin in 2:81 as another illustration.
  18:42/q06/p2 A garden is called ḥāʾiṭ because it surrounds its fruits or protects its owner. — reasons: Ibn al-Jawzi gives enclosure of many fruits; Ibn al-Anbari adds surrounding, benefiting and protecting the owner.
18:42/q07 What immediate calamity destroyed the garden? [وَأُحِيطَ بِثَمَرِهِۦ · reports] (turns on: Whether the notes specify a fire and vanishing water or only infer a sudden divine calamity from the scene.)
  18:42/q07/p1 God sent fire that burned it, and its water sank or disappeared. — reasons: Al-Tha'labi, al-Jishumi, al-Baghawi, al-Tabrisi, Abu Hayyan and Bursevi transmit or hold this account; al-Kashshaf reports the fire without water. Al-Alusi objects that the visible collapse makes a fire report unlikely unless the garden denotes the whole estate or the description means general ruin.
  18:42/q07/p2 A sudden, otherwise unspecified heavenly calamity annihilated the garden. — reasons: Al-Khafaji, as reported by al-Alusi, infers sudden destruction from the immediate morning scene; Islahi also speaks of a sudden calamity and fallen fences. Al-Hasan in Yahya says destruction enveloped it overnight; al-Qurtubi compares the garden of al-Qalam, blackened by morning.
18:42/q08 How does وَأُحِيطَ connect to the preceding narrative? [وَأُحِيطَ · grammar]
  18:42/q08/p1 It coordinates with an omitted event implied by the context. — reasons: Al-Alusi reports an unspoken earlier event before the clause of destruction.
18:42/q09 Does فَأَصْبَحَ mark morning or simply becoming? [فَأَصْبَحَ · meaning] (turns on: Whether aṣbaḥa retains its time-of-day sense or has the generalized sense 'became'.)
  18:42/q09/p1 Morning arrived after a night-time destruction. — reasons: Al-Hasan in Yahya says destruction came overnight. Ibn al-Jawzi's Nuzha groups this with al-Qalam 68:17 and 68:20 and cites 46:25; al-Qurtubi compares the sleeping garden owners whose garden was blackened by morning. Abu Hayyan says his awakening suggests night-time loss; al-Alusi and al-Khafaji infer the same from the immediate wording, and Islahi pictures him waking to ruin.
  18:42/q09/p2 It can mean 'became' without fixing the time of destruction. — reasons: Abu Hayyan says the morning inference is apparent but unnecessary; al-Samin and al-Alusi preserve both possibilities.
18:42/q10 What does his turning the two palms signify or do? [يُقَلِّبُ كَفَّيْهِ · interpretation] (turns on: Whether 'hand' names the actual physical gesture of remorse or figuratively denotes the property he surveys.)
  18:42/q10/p1 He makes a visible gesture of grief and regret over his lost spending. — reasons: Sources variously describe striking or clapping one hand against the other (Qatada, Ibn Abbas, al-Kalbi, al-Biqa'i), exposing palms then backs (Abu Hayyan, al-Alusi), placing palm against back of the other (Ibn Atiyya), or simply turning them. Ibn Atiyya specifically rejects 'clapping' as inaccurate. Al-Wahidi cites Arab usage, a poetic line and the parallel of biting a hand; Bursevi's Bahr al-'Ulum also cites biting fingertips and gnashing teeth. Al-Kashshaf, al-Samin and al-Alusi call it metaphor or metonym for remorse; al-Alusi distinguishes 'turning a matter inside out' as shifting topics. Al-Majaz, Ibn Qutayba and the others treat it as conventional idiom. Al-Tabari, Yahya, al-Razi, Ibn Kathir and al-Durr relate it to lost wealth; Bursevi quotes a Mathnawi couplet that grieving what is gone cannot restore it. Al-Itqan lists regret as a less familiar usage.
  18:42/q10/p2 He searches or surveys his estate for replacement wealth and finds 
<<part 0 ends; continues in part 1>>

<<18:42 update 1, part 1 of 0..2>>
none. — reasons: Al-Mawardi and al-Qurtubi report that 'hand' can mean property or dominion; the owner turns over what he owns, seeking compensation for the expense.
18:42/q11 Is there another reading of يُقَلِّبُ كَفَّيْهِ? [يُقَلِّبُ كَفَّيْهِ · readings]
  18:42/q11/p1 تُقَلَّبُ كَفَّاهُ: his two hands themselves are turned over. — reasons: Al-Samin reports the passive variant and gives its meaning; al-Alusi also notes the variant and says its mā can be verbal or relative.
18:42/q12 How does عَلَىٰ مَآ أَنفَقَ attach and express regret? [عَلَىٰ مَآ أَنفَقَ · grammar] (turns on: Whether the prepositional phrase attaches through an implied sense of regret or functions as a state description.)
  18:42/q12/p1 It attaches to يُقَلِّبُ because the verb implies regretting what was spent. — reasons: Al-Kashshaf says regret takes 'on'; al-Baydawi parses it as 'regretted what he spent'; Abu Hayyan, al-Samin and al-Alusi derive 'over' from the implied sense of remorse. Al-Alusi says this makes it grief over expenditure.
  18:42/q12/p2 The phrase can be a settled circumstantial modifier: he turns his hands while grieving. — reasons: Al-Alusi reports this alternative; treating the modifier as emphatic requires equating grief with regret, whereas some distinguish grief as narrower. Al-Samin reports Abu al-Baqa's omitted-phrase paraphrase of a regretful subject but says its formal parse is an unrestricted state.
18:42/q13 What expense does مَآ أَنفَقَ recall? [مَآ أَنفَقَ · referent]
  18:42/q13/p1 What he spent constructing, cultivating and improving the garden. — reasons: Al-Damghani specifies construction or cultivation; al-Kashshaf building, al-Nasafi cultivation, al-Biqa'i cultivation and improvement. Bursevi says regret over voluntary spending stands for grief over the acquired garden. Al-Alusi says the owner regretted this expenditure because he could have saved or used the money elsewhere, after trusting the garden would endure. Al-Razi says the loss is severe after a life spent seeking worldly gain at religion's expense.
18:42/q14 Does فِيهَا mean 'in' or 'on' the garden? [فِيهَا · meaning] (turns on: Whether fī is taken as a direct equivalent of ʿalā here or as a contextual extension of its locative sense.)
  18:42/q14/p1 Here fī means 'on' or 'upon' the garden. — reasons: Al-Tha'labi and al-Wahidi compare the Qur'anic wording for crucifying upon palm trunks (5:33 or 20:71); Ibn al-Jawzi's Nuzha calls this a recognized usage and notes 34:15; Ibn al-Jawzi's Zad states the equivalence here.
  18:42/q14/p2 The underlying sense is location within, extended metaphorically by context. — reasons: Ibn al-Jawzi's Nuzha states the base locative meaning and reports Abu Zakariyya on metaphorical uses such as being 'in' knowledge or work and possession pictured as being in the hand. Al-Wahidi notes that Arabic may speak of spending 'in' a house or garment as well as 'on' it.
18:42/q15 What can مَآ in مَآ أَنفَقَ mean? [مَآ أَنفَقَ · grammar] (turns on: Whether mā nominalizes the act of spending or refers to the thing spent.)
  18:42/q15/p1 A relative pronoun: what he spent. — reasons: Al-Alusi allows this on the variant reading where his hands are turned; the ordinary explanations also identify the lost money.
  18:42/q15/p2 A verbal noun: his spending. — reasons: Al-Alusi explicitly allows this alongside the relative sense on that variant reading.
18:42/q16 How did the garden lie خَاوِيَةٌ عَلَىٰ عُرُوشِهَا? [خَاوِيَةٌ عَلَىٰ عُرُوشِهَا · interpretation] (turns on: Whether ʿurūsh are vine frameworks or building roofs, and whether the walls also fell or remained standing.)
  18:42/q16/p1 The vine trellises fell and the vines or garden growth collapsed over them. — reasons: Al-Kashshaf, al-Nasafi, al-Baydawi and Bursevi identify grape supports and vines; al-Biqa'i says supports fell first, then what they carried. Al-Wahidi includes vine frameworks and building roofs. Al-Alusi defines ʿurūsh as vine supports and khāwiya as collapsed, and al-Qurtubi says both crop and framework perished. Al-Tabari and Muqatil describe fallen supports; al-Mawardi says foundation and produce both died.
  18:42/q16/p2 The roofs fell first, and the walls or structure collapsed over them. — reasons: Ibn Atiyya and al-Tabrisi explicitly sequence roof then wall; al-Razi reports roofs and walls as an alternative to vine arbors. Yahya reports the garden overturned onto roofs, and al-Mawardi says the garden was overturned. The phrase marks complete structural ruin.
  18:42/q16/p3 The walls remained standing but the roofs fell inside, leaving roofless buildings. — reasons: Al-Zajjaj describes roofless walls; al-Asamm in al-Jishumi gives this among roofless, dry and upside-down possibilities. Ibn al-Jawzi's Zad explicitly retains the walls while roofs have collapsed within; al-Jishumi says the remaining walls are useless.
  18:42/q16/p4 The site is empty of its plants, with bare soil or abandoned houses left. — reasons: Al-Hasan in Yahya says soil remained after plants vanished; al-Majaz glosses ʿurūsh as houses. Al-Tha'labi says plantings and buildings are gone; al-Tabrisi also reports empty houses after trees vanished. Ibn Qutayba calls khāwiya ruined and ʿurūsh roofs; al-Qurtubi notes usage for barren land, setting stars and collapsed houses. Al-Jishumi includes dryness.
  18:42/q16/p5 It broadly depicts an empty, overturned and ruined garden, without fixing the architecture. — reasons: Al-Farra allows fallen or empty on its roofs; al-Tabari, al-Tha'labi, al-Wahidi, al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Razi, al-Qurtubi, al-Biqa'i, Elmalili and Tabataba'i describe full collapse. Al-Razi says either arbor or roof interpretation yields complete ruin; Tabataba'i allows the root to mean falling or emptiness. The owner in Islahi finds the fences collapsed.
18:42/q17 Why are the vine trellises prominent in the ruin? [عُرُوشِهَا · rhetoric]
  18:42/q17/p1 The vines were the main planting, their ruin entailed the rest, or they cost the most to grow. — reasons: Al-Alusi reports these three explanations for singling out grapevines; Bursevi says the grape garden is singled out as the principal asset.
18:42/q18 How is وَيَقُولُ connected grammatically? [وَيَقُولُ · grammar] (turns on: Coordination versus a circumstantial wāw, whose use here al-Alusi calls rare.)
  18:42/q18/p1 It coordinates with يُقَلِّبُ. — reasons: Al-Samin and al-Alusi give this direct coordination.
  18:42/q18/p2 It is a circumstantial clause describing him while he turns his hands. — reasons: Al-Samin allows the state analysis; al-Alusi says it requires an implicit pronoun and notes the rarity of an affirmative present verb with circumstantial wāw.
18:42/q19 When does the owner say يَٰلَيْتَنِى لَمْ أُشْرِكْ? [وَيَقُولُ يَٰلَيْتَنِى · interpretation] (turns on: Whether the present narrative reports a speech immediately after worldly loss or anticipates a resurrection-day lament.)
  18:42/q19/p1 He says it in this life after the garden's destruction. — reasons: Ibn Atiyya allows worldly repentance after the calamity as a warning to Quraysh and others; Abu Hayyan prefers this apparent sense and the warning against faith delayed until punishment. Al-Wahidi, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Qurtubi and al-Nasafi say the regret is too late to help. Ibn Ashur sees the present tense as repeated regret after punishment.
  18:42/q19/p2 He says it in the Hereafter or on the Day of Resurrection. — reasons: Yahya places the speech in the Hereafter as a wish about his earlier life; Ibn Atiyya, Ibn al-Jawzi, Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi report this position. Al-Alusi notes that faith newly adopted on Judgment Day is unanimously useless.
18:42/q20 Is the wish sincere repentance or regret tied to lost wealth? [يَٰلَيْتَنِى لَمْ أُشْرِكْ بِرَبِّىٓ أَحَدًۭا · theology] (turns on: Whether he regrets shirk as sin and resolves to change, or wishes merely that monotheism had protected his wealth.)
  18:42/q20/p1 It is regret for lost worldly blessings, without accepted repentance or true faith. — reasons: Al-Jishumi says he wanted wealth preserved and that sincere repentance would have helped. Al-Razi says he wanted monotheism only to save the garden and God did not accept it. Al-Biqa'i says his thought remained confined to visible things; Bursevi likewise rejects sincerity. Al-Alusi rejects the faith interpretation: regretting disbelief alone is insufficient, he regretted the garden rather than the sin, and later context still denies resurrection. Al-Alusi cites al-Mawaqif that repentance requires resolve against returning and remorse for sin as sin. Al-Wahidi, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Qurtubi and al-Nasafi call the regret too late. Al-Razi says pursuit of worldly gain left him both material and religious loss.
  18:42/q20/p2 It may be repentance from shirk, remorse for past conduct and entry into faith. — reasons: Al-Kashshaf, al-Tabrisi, al-Nasafi, al-Baydawi and al-Alusi report this possibility; Ibn Atiyya allows worldly repentance. Ibn Ashur says the lament implies he now believes in God's oneness. Al-Alusi says regret over past shirk might imply present belief but argues against its adequacy.
18:42/q21 What does his admission of أُشْرِكْ mean? [أُشْرِكْ بِرَبِّىٓ أَحَدًۭا · interpretation] (turns on: Whether the confession is expressed as associationism generally or specified as dependence on created causes and personal achievement.)
  18:42/q21/p1 He recognizes that associating a partner, disbelieving or rebelling against God led to the calamity. — reasons: Al-Tabari says the unbeliever, left only with his deeds, regrets disbelief or shirk; al-Kashshaf, al-Razi, al-Nasafi, Abu Hayyan, Bursevi and al-Alusi connect the realization to his brother's admonition. Abu Hayyan says the brother's refusal to associate anyone had already indirectly accused him. Al-Qurtubi says he now recognizes the blessings came from God's power; al-Tha'labi and Muqatil give the straightforward confession. Ibn Ashur explains the vocative as anguish and laytani as

<<18:42 update 1, part 2 of 0..2>>
a wish personified and called to appear, comparing 39:56.
  18:42/q21/p2 His shirk included relying on the garden, himself, and worldly causes as independent powers. — reasons: Tabataba'i explicitly defines the shirk this way; Islahi says his arrogance treated the orchard as personal achievement and entitlement instead of God's gift demanding gratitude. Al-Qushayri contrasts one owner thanking the Creator with this owner disbelieving his Provider.
18:42/q22 How does the garden's ruin answer the believing companion's words? [* · links]
  18:42/q22/p1 It fulfills his warning and exposes the error of trusting wealth and worldly permanence. — reasons: Al-Mawardi, Abu Hayyan, Ibn Kathir and Study Quran link the loss to 18:40–41; al-Tabari recalls 18:35 and Abu Hayyan 18:32. Al-Nasafi says the owner remembered the warning; al-Tabrisi reports fire and the vanished water. Tabataba'i says the companion's words corrected his claim verbally while ruin demonstrated the error of permanence, followers and self-sufficiency. Al-Qushayri contrasts gratitude to the Creator with disbelief in the Provider. Islahi says he wakes to the collapse he thought impossible. Ibn Kathir and Study Quran note that the men or clan he boasted of in 18:34 cannot help him; Study Quran also cites 28:81.
18:42/q23 Where else is the expression about a garden fallen on its trellises discussed? [خَاوِيَةٌ عَلَىٰ عُرُوشِهَا · links]
  18:42/q23/p1 Abu Hayyan points back to the discussion at al-Baqara 2:259. — reasons: He refers to his earlier discussion of the same expression without adding another interpretation here.
18:42/q24 What does the owner's loss teach about punishment, trials and worldly attachment? [* · theology] (turns on: Whether the particular punishment is generalized into a rule about who suffers affliction; al-Razi denies that generalization.)
  18:42/q24/p1 The calamity answers his transgression and may benefit him by provoking regret. — reasons: Al-Mawardi and al-Qurtubi call it an answer to transgression; al-Jishumi says punishment can benefit the sinner by causing regret. Al-Razi says the man's life of worldly pursuit left both fortune and religious opportunity lost; al-Jishumi adds that loss of the self to eternal punishment warrants even greater regret. Ibn Kathir says neither clan nor the man himself could help, and God's authority was manifest.
  18:42/q24/p2 His ruin does not show that believers are exempt from suffering. — reasons: Al-Razi rejects that inference: believers also face many trials, and a prophetic report ranks prophets, saints and then the best as most tested; he mentions 43:33.
18:42/q25 What inward reading is given to the garden scene? [* · inward]
  18:42/q25/p1 The two gardens symbolize desire and world, their fruits cravings, and the owner's hand-turning regret for wasted life and potential. — reasons: Al-Nisaburi, as reported by al-Alusi, also reads wealth and status as inclinations and blameworthy traits, and expectation of a better garden as delusion about God.
18:42/q26 How are variant extra yāʾs in the sūra read? [* · readings]
  18:42/q26/p1 Nine of 37 extra yāʾs differ among readers. — reasons: Ibn Mujahid says Nafi' opens all listed forms except the three ma'i sabran; Abu 'Amr quiesces that trio and satajiduni; Ibn Kathir follows except min duni awliya'; Hafs opens the trio. The note concerns the wider sura rather than a word of this verse.
18:42/q27 Why does the written alif occur in لَٰكِنَّا هُوَ ٱللَّهُ رَبِّى? [* · readings]
  18:42/q27/p1 It reflects an original لكن أنا with deleted hamza and assimilated nūn. — reasons: Ibn Khalawayh says readers omit the alif in liaison on account of the nūn's fatḥa, while those retaining it at pause follow the written script. The phrase is from the neighboring passage.
18:42/q28 What principles and examples does al-Nashr give for major assimilation? [* · readings]
  18:42/q28/p1 Major assimilation lightens articulation, with detailed letter classes and counted examples. — reasons: Al-Nashr says the two letters remain articulated rather than literally entering one another, contrary to some; only manasikakum and ma salakakum assimilate within one word (2:200, 74:42). Alif and hamza neither assimilate nor accept assimilation. Its letter categories have five meeting no like, kind or neighbor; six meeting only identicals; five only kind or near letters; and eleven all, with totals 17 and 16. Ba' examples include la-dhahaba bi-sam'ihim and al-kitab bi-l-haqq, totaling 57 or 59 depending on joining sura endings to basmala. Ta' totals fourteen including finals becoming ha' at pause; tha' has three; ha' two including al-nikah hatta and wa-la abrahu hatta in al-Kahf; ra' totals 35; sin has three examples in al-Hajj and Nuh. These are broader reading notes.
18:42/q29 How are an apparent word's possible meanings resolved? [* · rhetoric]
  18:42/q29/p1 Verbal and contextual clues determine the intended sense; attached wording can redirect or clarify it. — reasons: Al-Burhan distinguishes words explicit in only one sense from apparent words permitting alternatives and gives 2:196 as an illustration.
18:42/q30 What does Ibn Ashur say about the origins and methods of tafsir? [* · sciences]
  18:42/q30/p1 Tafsir began with prophetic-era explanation and developed through transmitted and reasoned approaches. — reasons: Ibn Ashur says companions asked the Prophet meanings; prominent early interpreters include Ali, Ibn Abbas, Zayd, Ubayy, Ibn Mas'ud and Abdullah ibn Amr. Non-Arab converts increased the need, and he calls tafsir the foremost Islamic science. He says Ibn Jurayj (80–149 AH) first compiled it, gathering reports especially from Ibn Abbas's pupils Ata and Mujahid. Later approaches varied: Malik and al-Dawudi exemplify transmitted reports and al-Tabari their best-known extant representative; others reasoned or relied on Israelite stories, leading to fabricated material. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyya both examined Arabic and earlier views, the former emphasizing rhetoric and language, the latter law.
18:42/q31 How does Ibn Ashur assess early tafsir chains and claims about Ali? [* · reports]
  18:42/q31/p1 Several reports attributed to Ibn Abbas and Ali are unreliable; chains must be distinguished. — reasons: Ibn Ashur reports criticism of the al-Kalbi–Abu Salih route, Abu Salih's accusation of lying, and the addition of Muhammad ibn Marwan al-Suddi as a 'chain of lies,' contrasted with the Malik–Nafi'–Ibn Umar golden chain. He reports an allegation linking al-Kalbi to Abdullah ibn Saba's extreme claims that Ali would return. He prefers Ali ibn Abi Talha's Ibn Abbas reports over Muqatil and al-Dahhak because al-Bukhari used that route. He says fabricators hid behind Ibn Abbas's fame. Most reports attributed to Ali are fabricated unless soundly chained; Abu Juhaifa reports Ali denying extra family revelation beyond the Quran, while allowing God-granted understanding of it.
